description: A sea-crossing raft binds logs, bamboo or reed bundles into a platform buoyant enough to carry people over open water. No Pleistocene craft survives; such vessels are inferred from where people arrived. Settling Sahul, the joined landmass of Australia and New Guinea, required sea crossings by at least 50,000 years ago; the craft's form is unknown.
uncertainty: Arrival in Sahul is dated between roughly 50,000 and 65,000 years ago depending on the site and method; hominins on Flores about one million years ago imply a water crossing, but whether it was deliberate is contested. Raft form is inferred, not observed.

description: A dugout is a boat carved from a single large log, hollowed with stone adzes and sometimes with fire to char the wood for easier removal. The oldest preserved example, from Pesse in the Netherlands, dates to roughly 8,000 BCE. Sturdier than bark or reed craft, dugouts carried freight and fishers on lakes, rivers and estuaries.
uncertainty: Pesse is the oldest preserved dugout, not necessarily the first; radiocarbon dates cluster around the 9th-8th millennia BCE.

description: Celestial navigation with instruments measured the altitude of the Sun or the Pole Star with a mariner's astrolabe or quadrant, then corrected the reading with tables of solar declination. Portuguese pilots developed the practice in the late 15th century, as voyages south of the equator lost sight of the Pole Star. It gave latitude reliably, but not longitude.
uncertainty: The roles of particular scholars in preparing Portuguese declination tables are debated.

description: Longitude by chronometer compares local noon with the time kept by an accurate clock set to a reference meridian; each hour of difference equals 15 degrees. Pendulum clocks failed at sea. John Harrison's marine timekeeper H4 erred by only seconds on a 1761-62 trial voyage to Jamaica. Chronometers became common on ships during the 19th century.
uncertainty: The lunar-distance method offered a rival astronomical solution in the same decades; chronometers stayed costly for decades.

uncertainty: Many earlier screw designs were proposed; the 1836 patents mark practical development, not first invention.
